name: Adam Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to companies, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me your public view and, separately, what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a kitchen furniture factory, on the cabinet door line. I run a CNC router, which is a computer-controlled cutter that shapes the doors from big boards, and then an edge-bander that glues the trim on the edges. I load the boards, pick the right program off the screen, and check the doors for chips. Nine months in, and I still mix up the programs for the two shaker styles now and then.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing a full kitchen's worth of doors stacked at the end of the day. I've always liked wood, my grandad was a joiner. What wears me out is the dust mask and the foreman checking my numbers every hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I always thought it was mostly talk. I use a chatbot now and then to price my weekend joinery jobs, and it's handy, but that's it. At work it'd be a non-event.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means my plans stay on track. Rosa and I are getting married next summer, and I've got about seven months of pay saved, plus a share in a small rental flat with my dad. The factory needs people, and I'm getting better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, get my speed up, and ask the foreman about moving to the setter's role in a year or two. Keep doing small joinery jobs on Saturdays for extra money. Put the rental income towards the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job that bothers you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kitchen orders go up and down with house sales. When people stop moving house, we get fewer kitchen orders and the overtime goes. That's the real worry in my trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Rosa think of your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My fiancée Rosa thinks I should go full time as a joiner like my grandad. I tell her the factory pays steadier. Maybe one day.

Keep doing **Saturday joinery** jobs and put rental income towards the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good firms will use it well and bad ones won't. I'd say let businesses get on with it and keep the government out of the way. I'd probably mention it at the pub, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it hits the design office first. Kitchens are already drawn on computers, and AI would do the drawings and order the boards. On my line, I'd expect a robot arm to load the router within a few years, and that's half my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the setup side of the router once a couple of the lads have done it and say it's worth it. Use the chatbot a bit more for my joinery quotes. Keep the wedding date, keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's fine for now, but the line would change around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want the government out of the way. What if lots of people lose jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then families and churches step up, and firms should run apprenticeships. I don't like people being paid to sit at home, but paying them to learn a trade, I'd back that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your line would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our foreman Stan, who's 58 and hates screens. He knows wood better than anyone, but if the router starts setting itself, they won't need him to check our programs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for anyone, and the people who'll get through are the ones with real skills. I'd tell my mates to learn a proper trade. I'd want the government to fund apprenticeships, not cheques.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the router line is fully robotic by 2031. The AI in 2028 takes the design and ordering, and then three years later a robot loads, cuts and checks the doors. Fitting a kitchen in someone's old house, with crooked walls, feels a lot further off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first two years I'd start going out with a kitchen fitter on Saturdays to learn fitting. Keep the factory job until about 2030 for the pay. Scale the wedding down a bit and put the difference into tools and a van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got a way through, but the timing with the wedding is rough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd scale the wedding down. How does Rosa feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My fiancée Rosa would be fine with it, she's more practical than me. Her mum might not be. We'd still have it in her village church, just fewer guests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if robots can fit kitchens too, a few years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be doing repairs and odd jobs, the stuff nobody would build a robot for. There's always a door that won't shut in someone's house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning, and anyone sensible should be learning a hands-on trade now. I'd say firms should take on more apprentices. At the pub, mainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is about right for me. I'd keep the router job until about 2032, get married as planned, and build up the fitting work on the side. When robots come to the factory in 2034, I'd already be out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the factory job and have the wedding as planned. Do fitting on Saturdays from next year, and buy a van around 2029. Ask my dad whether we'd sell the rental flat to fund the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see a route, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI tools in your fitting business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once other fitters are using it, yes, for quotes and planning the jobs. I'm not going to be the first, but I won't be the last either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own kids one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids to learn with their hands and their heads. My grandad could fix anything with a chisel, and that's what got him through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone not to prepare. I'd tell young lads to get apprenticeships. I wouldn't make a big deal of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is good. I'd have time to become a setter, maybe a foreman, and then go out on my own as a fitter by my mid-thirties. The robots come in 2039 and I'd be 40, with my own business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get married, become the setter, and do joinery on the side. Use AI tools more once they're normal for small trades. Start my own fitting business around 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, slightly, in the background. Mostly I'd be looking forward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong for you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady pay is easy to stay with, so I'd get comfortable at the factory and forget to leave. Rosa would kick me if I did, to be fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want children in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, after the wedding, probably in two or three years. Ten years is enough to give them a stable start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it lands right on top of the wedding and our first years married. What would help is firms paying for apprenticeships in real trades, so people can switch without losing a year's wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people like me are proud of. I'm proud of making something you can touch, and I hope there's still room for that, robots or not.

headlineQuote: I'm proud of making something you can touch, and I hope there's still room for that, robots or not.
portrait: Adam is a **27-year-old** CNC router operator on a kitchen cabinet door line, nine months in.
He's engaged, with **seven months** saved and a share in a rental flat with his father.
He tries new tools once **others vouch** for them and favours apprenticeships over handouts.
As AGI nears he plans a move into **kitchen fitting**, timed around his wedding.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it lands on his **wedding** and first years married.
whatWouldHelp: Firms paying for **apprenticeships** in real trades, so switching costs no lost wages.
